scoreRule: 1 point per correct MC item; 10 points maximum; local provisional grade only
description: Independent ten-item B2 assessment draft for Why Did That Message Sound Rude?; human pedagogy approval required.

tabs.title: Applying the Argument
tabs.description: Use the text in new situations.

questions.q: Why can the message 'OK.' sound different from what the sender intended?
choices: Messages always follow formal punctuation rules.
A full stop means the sender is angry.
The receiver sees words without the tone and context of speech.
The sender must be travelling when writing it.
questions.explanation: The opening explains that typed text lacks voice, expressions and immediate clarification.

questions.q: What does the difference between young users' and older relatives' punctuation suggest?
choices: Digital signals are interpreted through different habits and expectations.
The older users are trying to sound unfriendly.
Punctuation has one fixed emotional meaning in every group.
Young users do not know what a full stop is.
questions.explanation: Paragraph two notes that the same mark may feel cold to one person and ordinary to another.

questions.q: What went wrong in Dana and Marek's group despite neither behaving rudely?
choices: Dana had forgotten to tell Marek about the present.
Marek had promised to order the book but never did.
The chat contained too many people to reach a decision.
Dana assumed an attitude Marek did not intend.
questions.explanation: Their different readings of 'fine' produced a delay without any deliberate offence.

questions.q: Why does the writer consider the time of a reply significant?
choices: Faster messages usually contain more accurate information.
Readers may mistake a practical delay for lack of interest.
A long delay means the sender cannot see the message.
After several hours the wording itself changes meaning.
questions.explanation: The same words may feel enthusiastic or indifferent depending on timing, despite an innocent reason for delay.

questions.q: Why would requiring long formal messages to friends be a poor solution?
choices: Every friend group would need its own dictionary.
Formal language is too difficult for most teenagers.
It could introduce an unnatural style and new misunderstandings.
It prevents people from speaking on the phone.
questions.explanation: Paragraph four explicitly rejects excessive formality as potentially strange and misleading.

questions.q: When is adding extra wording especially helpful?
choices: When a message involves decisions, disagreement or a person's feelings.
Whenever the sender is typing on a mobile phone.
Only when writing to a teacher or another adult.
When the whole group already agrees.
questions.explanation: The writer advises more explicit messages when the conversation matters.

questions.q: What is the advantage of asking 'Did you mean...?' rather than remaining silent?
choices: It guarantees the sender will apologise.
It makes a difficult conversation completely unnecessary.
It allows the recipient to interpret the message without an answer.
It checks an uncertain interpretation before conflict grows.
questions.explanation: The final paragraph advocates clarification over days of anxious assumptions.

questions.q: A group agrees that a thumbs-up means 'read, will reply later'. What does the agreement accomplish?
choices: It removes the need to read messages carefully.
It gives the same signal a shared interpretation.
It ensures everyone answers immediately.
It makes all messages less formal.
questions.explanation: The author says agreed signals can reduce doubt about whether a reply is pending.

questions.q: A classmate replies 'fine' to a suggested team activity. What is the best next step if the decision matters?
choices: Choose a different activity without asking.
Assume the classmate disliked the idea.
Ask whether they agree before changing the plan.
Wait two days before sending another message.
questions.explanation: The incident shows the cost of assuming a negative response instead of clarifying.

questions.q: Two friends are arguing about an emotional message. Which approach fits the conclusion?
choices: Talk by phone or in person so tone can be clarified.
Use even shorter replies until the argument ends.
Wait for the other person to guess the problem.
Ask someone else to post a screenshot.
questions.explanation: The conclusion recommends switching to voice or face-to-face discussion when the topic is emotional.
